chapterTitle: Unit Testing with Hardhat (Part 2: Interacting with Contracts & Events)
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute live coding video. Begin with the `AdvancedStorage.sol` contract. First, demonstrate how to get multiple signers and use `connect()` to send transactions from different accounts. Then, add tests for the `onlyOwner` modifier, showing both a successful call from the owner and a reverted call from a non-owner, using `to.be.revertedWith()`. Finally, add a test to verify the `DataChanged` event emission using `to.emit().withArgs()`. Use a split-screen view showing the code editor and the Hardhat test output in the terminal. Include a hands-on coding challenge where learners modify an existing test to add an event assertion.

screens.title: Interacting with Contracts & Events in Hardhat Tests
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to simulate real user interactions with smart contracts inside Hardhat tests. We focus on three practical capabilities: selecting which account sends a transaction, asserting that transactions revert with specific error messages, and verifying that contracts emit the expected events. These skills matter because production contracts rely on correct access control, precise error handling, and reliable event logs for off‑chain integrations. You'll see concrete examples using ethers. getSigners(), contract. connect(), the revertedWith matcher, and to. emit with withArgs so your tests confirm both behavior and telemetry. I will also highlight common mistakes like forgetting to await transactions or using non‑specific revert checks that can mask bugs. By the end you will be comfortable writing tests that exercise allowed and disallowed paths, checking state changes, and validating events for off‑chain consumers. To ground the ideas you will work through a token minting activity where only the owner may mint, and tests must assert balances, total supply, and Mint events. Keep a mindset of testing both the permitted path and the blocked path: that contrast is what proves your access control works. Ready to explore the exact patterns and example tests?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Tests must simulate different signers, assert specific revert messages, and verify emitted events to ensure correct access control and predictable off‑chain behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Interacting & Events
Interacting with Contracts & Events
Simulate signers, enforce access control, and confirm event logs.
In this lesson
You will practice getSigners, connect, revertedWith, and to.emit assertions using a token minting scenario.
// Example: connect a signer to send a transaction
const [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
await myContract.connect(owner).mint(addr1.address, 100);
await expect(myContract.connect(addr1).mint(addr1.address, 1))
  .to.be.revertedWith("Only owner can call this function");
await expect(myContract.connect(owner).mint(addr1.address, 50))
  .to.emit(myContract, "Mint").withArgs(addr1.address, 50);
Why it matters
Tests that precisely simulate accounts and events prevent regressions and protect user funds in production.
Key takeaway
Assert both permitted and blocked paths, and verify events for off‑chain listeners.
Visual Concept
Accounts (Signers)
A few signer cards represent owner and other accounts used to send transactions during tests.
Owner
Deploys contract and mints tokens; privileged actions.
Non-owner
Attempts blocked actions to ensure access control reverts correctly.
Explore Key Topics
Events, Reverts, Signers
Events: Assert emitted logs for off‑chain integrations.
Reverts: Test specific error messages with revertedWith.
Signers: Use getSigners and connect to simulate different senders.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will confidently write tests that simulate multiple accounts, verify access control, and check event emissions. First, you will learn to retrieve and use multiple signers so your tests represent different actors calling contract functions. Second, you will learn to send transactions from a specified account using the connect method, which is essential when msg. sender matters. Third, you will test for reverted transactions with a precise revert message, ensuring that failure cases are exact and easy to debug. Fourth, you will verify that contracts emit expected events with correct arguments so off‑chain listeners can depend on your logs. Each objective includes a practical example and a short mnemonic to help you remember the pattern. These skills reduce flakiness, prevent false positives, and reveal logic errors early. As you practice, focus on testing both allowed and disallowed paths and confirming state and logs after each transaction. The hands‑on activity at the end asks you to implement access‑controlled minting tests that illustrate all of these objectives in a single contract.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Checks
screens.narratorSegment: These practical checks will change how you think about unit tests. First, you will learn to assert state changes after transactions, not just that a call succeeded. That means checking balances, totals, and any emitted events. Second, you will learn to test both the happy path and the failure path. A passing test should prove that the allowed caller can change state and that a disallowed caller triggers the specific revert message you expect. Third, you will understand why specific revert messages are more useful than generic revert checks: they ensure the failure reason matches your contract logic and help debugging. Fourth, you will learn to test events with exact argument matching so off‑chain services that parse logs can rely on your contract. These objectives together make tests that are both trustworthy and diagnostic. In the hands‑on token minting activity, you will exercise each of these checks by verifying owner-only minting, total supply updates, balance changes, and the Mint event with the correct arguments.

keyIdea.title: Practical testing focus
keyIdea.text: Assert state, test both allowed and blocked paths, prefer specific revert messages, and verify event arguments.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Practical Checks
Objective: Assert state changes
After transactions, read contract state and assert exact values such as balances and totals.
Example
Owner mints 100 tokens to addr1; assert totalSupply increases by 100 and balanceOf(addr1) equals 100.
Misconception
Only checking that a transaction does not throw can miss silent logic errors; assert the resulting state explicitly.
Objective: Test event payloads
Use withArgs to confirm event arguments so off‑chain indexers see correct data.
Example
Expect a Mint event with to address and amount when owner mints tokens.
Misconception
Checking only that an event emitted without verifying args can allow incorrect payloads to slip through.
Check both sides
Every access‑controlled function should have at least one test for the allowed caller and one for a disallowed caller that reverts with the expected message.

screens.title: Signers and msg.sender: How tests simulate accounts
screens.narratorSegment: A signer represents an Ethereum account that can sign and send transactions inside a test environment. In Hardhat, ethers. getSigners() returns an array of Signer objects you can use to represent different actors: the deployer, a second user, and so on. This matters because many contract functions rely on msg. sender to enforce permissions or record who performed an action. If your test always sends transactions from the default deployer, you may miss bugs where a non‑owner should be blocked. Practically, you destructure signers like const [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers. getSigners(); and then use owner. address in assertions or connect(owner) to send a transaction from that account. A concrete example: if an owner‑only function should succeed for owner and fail for addr1, using getSigners lets you simulate both actors in the same test suite. A common misconception is to treat Signer like a plain address string; Signer can send transactions and sign messages, so you must use contract. connect(signer) when you want the transaction to be from that account. To test thoroughly, always exercise both allowed and blocked callers, check the state changes after successful calls, and confirm that blocked calls revert with the intended message. How will you structure your next test to include at least two signers and a clear allowed vs blocked path?

keyIdea.title: Definition: Signer
keyIdea.text: A Signer is an object that represents an account capable of signing and sending transactions in Hardhat tests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Signers
What is a Signer?
A Signer is an ethers object that can sign transactions and messages. Use it to simulate an account sending a transaction so msg.sender in the contract matches the expected caller.
Code snippet
const [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers.getSigners();
// owner, addr1, and addr2 are Signer objects
Concrete example
Use owner to deploy and grant rights, then simulate addr1 attempting a privileged operation to ensure it reverts as expected.
Common mistake
Using only address strings and not Signer.connect for transactions means the call will not originate from the intended account.
Practical checks
  • Always destructure getSigners in beforeEach so tests share the same signer fixtures.
  • Use signer.address when you need the raw address for assertions or event arg checks.
  • Use contract.connect(signer) when sending transactions to set msg.sender correctly.
Key Takeaway

Signers let your tests impersonate accounts; use connect to ensure msg.sender is accurate and simulate both allowed and denied calls.

screens.title: Using contract.connect(signer) to send transactions
screens.narratorSegment: When you need a transaction to come from a specific account, contract. connect(signer) is the explicit tool you use. The pattern is straightforward: retrieve signers, deploy from the desired deployer signer, then call contract. connect(otherSigner). functionToCall(args). For example, to test that only the owner can set stored data, deploy with the owner signer and then call set through both owner and another signer. The owner call should succeed and update state; the non‑owner call should revert. A concrete example from the chapter shows advancedStorage. connect(owner). set(500) followed by expect(advancedStorage. connect(addr1). set(501)). to. be. revertedWith("Only owner can call this function"). Remember to await transactions so the test waits for mining and the state update. A common misconception is thinking connect changes a persistent signer on the contract; connect returns a transient contract instance bound to that signer for that call. Another gotcha is deploying with the wrong signer — deploy via ContractFactory with the intended deployer to ensure owner is set properly in the constructor. After you call connect and send a transaction, always read back the relevant getter to assert the state change. Try structuring tests with explicit connect calls for both success and failure paths to make the intent clear.

keyIdea.title: Pattern: connect(signer)
keyIdea.text: Use contract.connect(signer) to execute a transaction as a particular account and then assert state changes or reverts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › contract.connect()
Two-step pattern
  1. Get signers: const [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
  2. Deploy with owner: Factory = await ethers.getContractFactory("Contract", owner);
  3. Send transaction: await contract.connect(owner).set(500);
  4. Assert state: expect(await contract.get()).to.equal(500);
Transient instance note
connect returns a new contract instance bound to that signer; it does not change the original instance globally.
Example test card
it("Only owner can set a value", async function () {
  await advancedStorage.connect(owner).set(500);
  expect(await advancedStorage.get()).to.equal(500);
  await expect(advancedStorage.connect(addr1).set(501))
    .to.be.revertedWith("Only owner can call this function");
});
Pro tip

When deploying, pass the intended owner to getContractFactory so constructor owner matches the test expectation.

screens.title: Reverts and revertedWith: testing failures precisely
screens.narratorSegment: A revert occurs when a contract executes a require, revert, or assert that fails; the EVM rolls back state changes and the transaction does not persist. In tests, it is vital to check for reverts so you confirm that invalid actions are blocked. More importantly, use the revertedWith matcher to assert the exact revert message. This precision ensures that your test fails if a different check triggers or if the message changes unexpectedly. For example, await expect(contract. connect(addr1). set(value)). to. be. revertedWith("Only owner can call this function") confirms that the onlyOwner modifier fired. A common mistake is to use a generic to. be. reverted because it only says a revert happened and doesn't say which condition caused it, which can mask regressions. Another pitfall is forgetting to await the expect call; since expect returns a promise you must await it so the test waits for the revert assertion. Concrete scenario: if set requires x!= storedData and onlyOwner, write separate tests for both conditions: one where the owner sets the same value to check the new-data requirement and another where a non‑owner attempts to set and triggers onlyOwner. Ending question: when you write a test for a revert, can you name the exact message that proves the right condition failed?

keyIdea.title: Testing failures
keyIdea.text: Use to.be.revertedWith("message") to verify both that a call reverted and that it failed for the expected reason.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Reverts
What is a revert?
A revert undoes state changes and indicates a failed precondition. Tests should assert both occurrence and specific reason.
Example: onlyOwner fallback
await expect(advancedStorage.connect(addr1).set(100))
  .to.be.revertedWith("Only owner can call this function");
Testing multiple failure reasons
Write distinct tests for each require condition to ensure every guard works as intended, for example new-data versus only-owner.
Common mistake

Do not use a generic revert check. Be explicit about the expected message so the test documents intent and catches the right guard.

Quick checklist
  • Use await expect(...).to.be.revertedWith("message").
  • Write tests for each precondition separately.
  • Avoid swallowing asynchronous errors by forgetting await.
Reflection
Which revert messages in your contracts are important to assert to prevent silent logic errors?

screens.title: Events and to.emit(...).withArgs(...)
screens.narratorSegment: Events are structured logs that contracts emit so off‑chain services can react to on‑chain changes. Testing events ensures those logs contain the expected information and ordering. In Hardhat tests use expect(transaction). to. emit(contract, "EventName"). withArgs(arg1, arg2,...). First, call the function that should emit the event, then assert the emission and provide the expected argument values. For example, after a successful mint you might write await expect(myToken. connect(owner). mint(addr1. address, 100)). to. emit(myToken, "Mint"). withArgs(addr1. address, 100). This verifies both the name and the exact payload. A typical misconception is relying on a generic to. emit without withArgs — that confirms an event occurred but not that it carried the correct values. Another nuance is that indexed event fields are stored differently in the log; however, withArgs still checks the effective arguments you expect in the order declared. Also test events alongside state checks: after asserting the Mint event, verify totalSupply and balances to ensure logs and state align. Closing thought: what off‑chain workflows will consume your events, and what fields must they trust? Events and to.emit(...).withArgs(...) means use to.emit(contract, "name").withargs(...) to assert both that an event occurred and that its arguments match expectations.. In practical terms, verify logs emitted by contracts so off‑chain systems can trust them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event check
keyIdea.text: Use to.emit(contract, "Name").withArgs(...) to assert both that an event occurred and that its arguments match expectations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Events
Why test events?
Events are the contract's public logbook. Off‑chain systems read these logs to index state changes, trigger notifications, or update databases. Tests ensure those logs are trustworthy.
Example assertion
await expect(myToken.connect(owner).mint(addr1.address, 100))
  .to.emit(myToken, "Mint")
  .withArgs(addr1.address, 100);
Follow this with state checks: expect(await myToken.totalSupply()).to.equal(100); expect(await myToken.balanceOf(addr1.address)).to.equal(100);
Common pitfalls
  • Checking only that an event emitted without verifying args.
  • Assuming order of arguments or forgetting to use the address property of signers for comparisons.
  • Forgetting to await the expect call that checks emission.
Key Takeaway

Events are testable contracts of intent. Verify both emission and payloads to keep on‑chain logs dependable for off‑chain consumers.

screens.title: Example: AdvancedStorage tests reviewed
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the AdvancedStorage tests step by step to illustrate the patterns we've discussed. First, in beforeEach we call ethers. getSigners() to obtain owner, addr1, and addr2 and deploy the contract with the owner signer. This establishes owner in the constructor. The first test calls advancedStorage. connect(owner). set(500) then asserts the getter returns 500, demonstrating a successful state change. The second test switches context and uses expect(advancedStorage. connect(addr1). set(501)). to. be. revertedWith("Only owner can call this function") to prove the access control blocks non‑owners. Next, the event test reads the oldValue using await advancedStorage. get(), then sends a set with the owner and asserts to. emit(advancedStorage, "DataChanged"). withArgs(oldValue, newValue, owner. address). This checks the event name and three arguments exactly. An important detail is to await both transaction promises and the expect assertions so tests wait for mining and the matcher chain. A common misconception is assuming the event arguments will be plain numbers or objects—use the same types your contract emits, such as addresses and indexed values, and compare them accordingly. After this walkthrough, consider how you would refactor a failing test to reveal whether it was a deployment mismatch, a signer misuse, or an off‑by‑one assertion error.

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough insight
keyIdea.text: Explicitly await transactions and use connect to test allowed and blocked paths, and use withArgs to assert event payloads exactly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › AdvancedStorage Walkthrough
Test structure
beforeEach sets signers and deploys with owner. Each it block then uses connect to simulate callers and asserts state or reverts.
beforeEach(async function () {
  [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers.getSigners();
  AdvancedStorage = await ethers.getContractFactory("AdvancedStorage", owner);
  advancedStorage = await AdvancedStorage.deploy();
});

it("Should allow only owner to set a value", async function () {
  await advancedStorage.connect(owner).set(500);
  expect(await advancedStorage.get()).to.equal(500);
  await expect(advancedStorage.connect(addr1).set(501))
    .to.be.revertedWith("Only owner can call this function");
});
Note how both state assertions and revert assertions appear together. This combination documents expected behavior and failure modes clearly.
Event test snippet
await expect(advancedStorage.connect(owner).set(newValue))
  .to.emit(advancedStorage, "DataChanged")
  .withArgs(oldValue, newValue, owner.address);
Confirm both the event and the state. If the event args differ, the withArgs assertion will fail and point to the mismatch.

screens.title: Common testing mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes that make tests flaky or falsely passing. First, forgetting to await a transaction or an expect matcher causes the test runner to move on before the blockchain state updates, leading to race conditions or silent failures. For example, omitting await before expect(...). to. be. revertedWith() can make a test pass incorrectly. Second, using a generic to. be. reverted rather than to. be. revertedWith("message") hides which condition failed and can mask a different failing guard. Third, not using contract. connect(signer) and instead calling functions through the default signer causes tests to use the deployer account unintentionally. This often results in tests that appear to pass but do not simulate real attackers. Fourth, deploying with the wrong signer means owner will not match expectations; always pass the intended signer to getContractFactory when you want a particular owner. To avoid these mistakes, adopt a checklist: always await transactions and expect clauses, write explicit revert messages for each require, use connect for non‑deployer calls, and assert both the state and emitted events. A healthy practice is to write minimal tests that fail first, then implement the contract logic until the tests pass, which helps ensure the test is exercising the intended behavior. Which checklist item would you add to your test template?

A healthy practice is to write minimal tests that fail first, then implement the contract logic until the tests pass, which helps ensure the test is exercising the intended behavior. Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Common Mistakes
Mistake: Missing await
Always await both transactions and expect matcher chains to ensure the test waits for the network action and assertion to complete.
Example failure mode: a test appears green but actually never awaited the promise that would reveal the revert.
Mistake: Generic revert checks
Using to.be.reverted does not prove which guard triggered. Use revertedWith to be explicit about intent.

  • Use connect(signer) for non‑deployer callers.

screens.narratorSegment: The hands‑on activity asks you to create a MyToken contract and four unit tests that demonstrate the patterns we've discussed. Your test plan should include: 1) an initial deployment test that verifies totalSupply is zero and owner is set correctly, 2) an owner mint test that mints to addr1 and asserts totalSupply, balances, and the Mint event, 3) a non‑owner mint test that expects a revert with "Only owner can call this function", and 4) a test that mints to the zero address and expects a revert with "Cannot mint to zero address". Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Activity: MyToken
Test plan
  1. Deploy: assert totalSupply === 0 and owner is set.
  2. Owner mints: call connect(owner).mint(addr1, amount); assert totalSupply and balanceOf, and assert Mint event.
  3. Non-owner mint: expect connect(addr1).mint(... ) to.be.revertedWith("Only owner can call this function").

  MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken", owner);
  myToken = await MyToken.deploy();
});

// Then implement the four tests described above

await expect(myToken.connect(owner).mint(addr1.address, 1000))
  .to.emit(myToken, "Mint").withArgs(addr1.address, 1000);

screens.title: Structuring tests for clarity and reliability
screens.narratorSegment: Well-structured tests are easier to maintain and reveal the exact reason a test failed. Start each test file with a beforeEach that gets signers and deploys the contract with the intended deployer signer. This keeps setup consistent and minimizes repeated code. Adopt the arrange-act-assert pattern in each it block: arrange the preconditions, act by sending the transaction with connect(signer), then assert state, events, or reverts. Use descriptive test names such as "owner can mint tokens" and "non-owner cannot mint tokens" so test output communicates intent. Keep tests focused: each it should exercise one behavior or one guard so failures map directly to a single contract obligation. For example, separate the onlyOwner guard test from the new-data-check test rather than combining them. When you need to test multiple reverts for the same function, write distinct tests for each require message. If you see flakiness, add explicit awaits and consider isolating a failing test to reproduce the issue more easily. Also include event assertions alongside state checks for a complete verification of both on‑chain state and off‑chain signals. Finally, consider whether test helpers or fixtures can reduce duplication while preserving test clarity. Do your test names and structure make debugging faster?

screens.title: Testing edge cases: zero address and multiple event checks
screens.narratorSegment: Edge cases often hide bugs that only appear in production. Two important edge cases discussed in this chapter are zero‑address validation and verifying multiple emitted events. For zero-address checks, contracts should prevent minting to address(0) because it can lock tokens irretrievably. In your tests, explicitly attempt to mint to ethers. constants. AddressZero or the string '0x000...0' and expect a revert with the contract's specified message such as "Cannot mint to zero address". Testing this confirms your guard against invalid recipients. For multiple events, some functions emit several events—for example, minting might emit both Mint and Transfer to follow ERC20 semantics. Your test can either assert both events separately or assert one event and then inspect the transaction receipt to programmatically check additional logs. However, prefer the matched assertions with to. emit(...). withArgs(...) where practical because they read clearly in tests. Also consider ordering: if two events must occur in a particular order, write assertions that reflect that ordering or check the receipt logs accordingly. Finally, ensure your tests remain readable: isolate edge-case tests so failures point to specific limitations. After adding these checks, run the test suite to see if any unhandled edge cases appear and fix the contract where necessary.

screens.title: Assessment idea and test validation patterns
screens.narratorSegment: To validate learning, use short assessment questions and practical validation steps. A good multiple‑choice question asks which snippet correctly tests that a non‑owner cannot call a privileged function. The correct pattern uses connect(nonOwnerAccount) and to. be. revertedWith with the expected message. The distractors typically omit connect, misuse synchronous throw matchers, or test for event absence rather than revert. For practical validation, run the test suite and inspect failing traces. If a revert assertion fails, confirm which require fired by temporarily emitting diagnostic events or logging in the contract during debugging. Another validation step is to run tests with different signers in a single file to ensure isolation. When an event assertion fails, compare the actual transaction receipt logs to the expected args and types; mismatches usually indicate an off‑by‑one in argument order or incorrect address formatting. Finally, treat tests as documentation: clear test names and explicit assertions make it easier for a reviewer to verify behavior without reading the contract deeply. As a next exercise, adapt an existing test by adding an event assertion and running the suite to see how it tightens coverage.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to simulate real user interactions with smart contracts inside Hardhat tests. We focus on three practical capabilities: selecting which account sends a transaction, asserting that transactions revert with specific error messages, and verifying that contracts emit the expected events. These skills matter because production contracts rely on correct access control, precise error handling, and reliable event logs for off‑chain integrations. You'll see concrete examples using ethers. getSigners(), contract. connect(), the revertedWith matcher, and to. emit with withArgs so your tests confirm both behavior and telemetry. I will also highlight common mistakes like forgetting to await transactions or using non‑specific revert checks that can mask bugs. By the end you will be comfortable writing tests that exercise allowed and disallowed paths, checking state changes, and validating events for off‑chain consumers. To ground the ideas you will work through a token minting activity where only the owner may mint, and tests must assert balances, total supply, and Mint events. Keep a mindset of testing both the permitted path and the blocked path: that contrast is what proves your access control works. Ready to explore the exact patterns and example tests?

By the end of this chapter you will confidently write tests that simulate multiple accounts, verify access control, and check event emissions. First, you will learn to retrieve and use multiple signers so your tests represent different actors calling contract functions. Second, you will learn to send transactions from a specified account using the connect method, which is essential when msg. sender matters. Third, you will test for reverted transactions with a precise revert message, ensuring that failure cases are exact and easy to debug. Fourth, you will verify that contracts emit expected events with correct arguments so off‑chain listeners can depend on your logs. Each objective includes a practical example and a short mnemonic to help you remember the pattern. These skills reduce flakiness, prevent false positives, and reveal logic errors early. As you practice, focus on testing both allowed and disallowed paths and confirming state and logs after each transaction. The hands‑on activity at the end asks you to implement access‑controlled minting tests that illustrate all of these objectives in a single contract.

These practical checks will change how you think about unit tests. First, you will learn to assert state changes after transactions, not just that a call succeeded. That means checking balances, totals, and any emitted events. Second, you will learn to test both the happy path and the failure path. A passing test should prove that the allowed caller can change state and that a disallowed caller triggers the specific revert message you expect. Third, you will understand why specific revert messages are more useful than generic revert checks: they ensure the failure reason matches your contract logic and help debugging. Fourth, you will learn to test events with exact argument matching so off‑chain services that parse logs can rely on your contract. These objectives together make tests that are both trustworthy and diagnostic. In the hands‑on token minting activity, you will exercise each of these checks by verifying owner-only minting, total supply updates, balance changes, and the Mint event with the correct arguments.

A signer represents an Ethereum account that can sign and send transactions inside a test environment. In Hardhat, ethers. getSigners() returns an array of Signer objects you can use to represent different actors: the deployer, a second user, and so on. This matters because many contract functions rely on msg. sender to enforce permissions or record who performed an action. If your test always sends transactions from the default deployer, you may miss bugs where a non‑owner should be blocked. Practically, you destructure signers like const [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers. getSigners(); and then use owner. address in assertions or connect(owner) to send a transaction from that account. A concrete example: if an owner‑only function should succeed for owner and fail for addr1, using getSigners lets you simulate both actors in the same test suite. A common misconception is to treat Signer like a plain address string; Signer can send transactions and sign messages, so you must use contract. connect(signer) when you want the transaction to be from that account. To test thoroughly, always exercise both allowed and blocked callers, check the state changes after successful calls, and confirm that blocked calls revert with the intended message. How will you structure your next test to include at least two signers and a clear allowed vs blocked path?

When you need a transaction to come from a specific account, contract. connect(signer) is the explicit tool you use. The pattern is straightforward: retrieve signers, deploy from the desired deployer signer, then call contract. connect(otherSigner). functionToCall(args). For example, to test that only the owner can set stored data, deploy with the owner signer and then call set through both owner and another signer. The owner call should succeed and update state; the non‑owner call should revert. A concrete example from the chapter shows advancedStorage. connect(owner). set(500) followed by expect(advancedStorage. connect(addr1). set(501)). to. be. revertedWith("Only owner can call this function"). Remember to await transactions so the test waits for mining and the state update. A common misconception is thinking connect changes a persistent signer on the contract; connect returns a transient contract instance bound to that signer for that call. Another gotcha is deploying with the wrong signer — deploy via ContractFactory with the intended deployer to ensure owner is set properly in the constructor. After you call connect and send a transaction, always read back the relevant getter to assert the state change. Try structuring tests with explicit connect calls for both success and failure paths to make the intent clear.

A revert occurs when a contract executes a require, revert, or assert that fails; the EVM rolls back state changes and the transaction does not persist. In tests, it is vital to check for reverts so you confirm that invalid actions are blocked. More importantly, use the revertedWith matcher to assert the exact revert message. This precision ensures that your test fails if a different check triggers or if the message changes unexpectedly. For example, await expect(contract. connect(addr1). set(value)). to. be. revertedWith("Only owner can call this function") confirms that the onlyOwner modifier fired. A common mistake is to use a generic to. be. reverted because it only says a revert happened and doesn't say which condition caused it, which can mask regressions. Another pitfall is forgetting to await the expect call; since expect returns a promise you must await it so the test waits for the revert assertion. Concrete scenario: if set requires x!= storedData and onlyOwner, write separate tests for both conditions: one where the owner sets the same value to check the new-data requirement and another where a non‑owner attempts to set and triggers onlyOwner. Ending question: when you write a test for a revert, can you name the exact message that proves the right condition failed?

Events are structured logs that contracts emit so off‑chain services can react to on‑chain changes. Testing events ensures those logs contain the expected information and ordering. In Hardhat tests use expect(transaction). to. emit(contract, "EventName"). withArgs(arg1, arg2,...). First, call the function that should emit the event, then assert the emission and provide the expected argument values. For example, after a successful mint you might write await expect(myToken. connect(owner). mint(addr1. address, 100)). to. emit(myToken, "Mint"). withArgs(addr1. address, 100). This verifies both the name and the exact payload. A typical misconception is relying on a generic to. emit without withArgs — that confirms an event occurred but not that it carried the correct values. Another nuance is that indexed event fields are stored differently in the log; however, withArgs still checks the effective arguments you expect in the order declared. Also test events alongside state checks: after asserting the Mint event, verify totalSupply and balances to ensure logs and state align. Closing thought: what off‑chain workflows will consume your events, and what fields must they trust? Events and to.emit(...).withArgs(...) means use to.emit(contract, "name").withargs(...) to assert both that an event occurred and that its arguments match expectations.. In practical terms, verify logs emitted by contracts so off‑chain systems can trust them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the AdvancedStorage tests step by step to illustrate the patterns we've discussed. First, in beforeEach we call ethers. getSigners() to obtain owner, addr1, and addr2 and deploy the contract with the owner signer. This establishes owner in the constructor. The first test calls advancedStorage. connect(owner). set(500) then asserts the getter returns 500, demonstrating a successful state change. The second test switches context and uses expect(advancedStorage. connect(addr1). set(501)). to. be. revertedWith("Only owner can call this function") to prove the access control blocks non‑owners. Next, the event test reads the oldValue using await advancedStorage. get(), then sends a set with the owner and asserts to. emit(advancedStorage, "DataChanged"). withArgs(oldValue, newValue, owner. address). This checks the event name and three arguments exactly. An important detail is to await both transaction promises and the expect assertions so tests wait for mining and the matcher chain. A common misconception is assuming the event arguments will be plain numbers or objects—use the same types your contract emits, such as addresses and indexed values, and compare them accordingly. After this walkthrough, consider how you would refactor a failing test to reveal whether it was a deployment mismatch, a signer misuse, or an off‑by‑one assertion error.

A healthy practice is to write minimal tests that fail first, then implement the contract logic until the tests pass, which helps ensure the test is exercising the intended behavior. AddressZero or the string '0x000...0' and expect a revert with the contract's specified message such as "Cannot mint to zero address". Testing this confirms your guard against invalid recipients. For multiple events, some functions emit several events—for example, minting might emit both Mint and Transfer to follow ERC20 semantics. Your test can either assert both events separately or assert one event and then inspect the transaction receipt to programmatically check additional logs. However, prefer the matched assertions with to. emit(...). withArgs(...) where practical because they read clearly in tests. Also consider ordering: if two events must occur in a particular order, write assertions that reflect that ordering or check the receipt logs accordingly. Finally, ensure your tests remain readable: isolate edge-case tests so failures point to specific limitations.
